analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for day care providers to lie to parents or seriously injure children through recklessness.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced with bipartisan support in February 1999, it sat in the House Judiciary Committee's Crime Subcommittee for nearly two years, got one hearing, and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Jeremy and Julia's Law would amend federal criminal law to penalize child day care providers. A provider who knowingly makes false statements about the care, the provider, or an employee — to a parent deciding where to place a child, or to police — in a way that puts a child's safety or health at substantial risk, could be fined or imprisoned up to one year. A provider who recklessly causes serious bodily injury to a child could be fined or imprisoned up to three years. The bill applied to providers 'in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce.'
analysis.who_benefits: Parents choosing day care, and the children placed in it. The bill would give families a federal remedy when a provider lies to them about the care they are buying, and would add a federal penalty on top of state law when recklessness causes a child serious injury.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and children in day care

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a day care provider or employee from knowingly making false statements about the care, the provider, or an employee to a parent or guardian considering placement, when that lie places a child's safety or health at substantial risk, punishable by fine or up to one year in prison.
Makes it a federal crime, punishable by fine or up to three years in prison, for a day care provider to recklessly cause a child serious bodily injury.
Covers any person or entity providing day care in a place other than the child's own home, so it reaches commercial and center-based providers as well as family-style care outside the home.

analysis.who_pays: Day care providers and their employees who misrepresent their care or act recklessly — through federal fines and prison terms. Honest, careful providers would face no new obligation beyond not lying and not being reckless.
analysis.who_pays_short: Day care providers who misrepresent or endanger children

drawbacks.text: The maximum penalties are modest — one year for deceptive representations and three years for reckless serious injury — and they overlap with fraud, child endangerment, and negligence laws that most states already enforce, raising the question of what a federal layer adds beyond what a state prosecutor could seek.

The bill reaches only providers 'in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce,' a hook that determines which cases fall under federal rather than state jurisdiction and could leave purely local situations to state law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: parents deciding where to leave their child would gain a federal penalty against providers who lie to them in ways that endanger children, and recklessness causing serious injury would carry a federal term. The costs are limited to providers who actually misrepresent their care or injure children recklessly, and the penalties are modest relative to the harm. The main honest objection is duplication — states already prosecute fraud and child endangerment — but the bill is narrowly drawn and poses little risk to careful providers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee — it was referred to the subcommittee three weeks after introduction, got a single hearing in October 2000, and never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Rick Lazio of New York introduced Jeremy and Julia's Law in the House on February 2, 1999.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
On February 25, 1999, the Judiciary Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Crime, where it remained.
The Subcommittee on Crime held hearings on the bill on October 4, 2000 — the only substantive action the bill received in its twenty-three months of life.
No markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever followed; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Day care providers who misrepresent their care, and providers who endanger children through recklessness, are better off: no federal penalty was ever enacted. Parents and children gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Providers the bill would have penalized

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines from the start: the sponsor was a Republican, an original cosponsor was a Democrat, and the full cosponsor list of 15 split 9 Democrats and 6 Republicans. The bill received no recorded votes, so no party split is visible in the record; what stalled it was committee inaction, not a party-line fight.

industries.note: The bill would create federal criminal liability for providers who lie to parents about their care in ways that endanger children, and for recklessness causing serious injury. Law-abiding providers would be untouched; only those who misrepresent care or endanger children would face fines or prison.
